idiom_name: passkey token: empty class with a private constructor plus friend T (More C++ Idioms / Chromium base::PassKey)
implementation_notes: Friendship is all-or-nothing - a friend declaration grants access to every private member - so instead of friending the collaborator, the restricted class accepts an empty token parameter and the token declares the collaborator as its friend: template <typename T> class PassKey { friend T; PassKey() = default; };. Only that collaborator can construct the token (Chromium's base::PassKey is exactly this), the parameter is left unnamed to show it carries no semantics, and passing it by value is effectively free at run time. The token need not be nested, so one shared key type can authorise operations of several classes. Keep the default and copy constructors genuinely private: on pre-C++20 toolchains aggregate initialisation could build an empty key with a defaulted private constructor, and a public copy constructor allows minting one from a null-pointer dereference.
pitfalls: A defaulted private default constructor on an empty key class can be bypassed by aggregate initialisation before C++20; give the key a user-provided constructor and keep the copy constructor private too.
Making the key's constructor public (or befriending more types in the key) turns the token into an ordinary argument anyone can supply.

friend T in the key authorises the whole type T, not one function; if only one member function of the collaborator should mint keys, add a private static factory instead of widening the friend declaration.

variants.name: Concept-constrained multi-type key (C++20)
variants.idiom_name: base::PassKey<Args...>: one key authorising a whole group, with implicit subset conversion
variants.implementation_notes: Chromium's current pass_key.h generalises the token to a variadic key: PassKey<A, B> can be built from PassKey<A> or PassKey<B> when the source's authorised set is a subset of the target's, the arguments must be pairwise unique (enforced by a concept and a static_assert), and the subset conversion is implicit precisely so that a key for one collaborator can be fed to an operation expecting a group. Choose it when one operation is legitimately open to a set of collaborators rather than to a single type, or when a group key should be derivable from the individual keys instead of re-declared per caller.
pitfalls: The subset conversion is implicit on purpose, so a group key quietly accepts any individual key of the group - do not declare a group key where a single collaborator was meant.
requires-clauses and concepts make the header C++20-only; on older toolchains the classic friend-token remains the right variant.
Multi-type keys widen the authorised set at compile time, so a reviewer must read the concept-constrained conversion rather than a single friend declaration.

variants.name: Non-copyable token (C++11)
variants.idiom_name: base::NonCopyablePassKey: key with deleted copy and move, so the grant cannot be delegated
variants.implementation_notes: Deleting the key's copy and move operations makes the grant non-transitive: a function that receives a key can call the restricted operation but cannot store, copy or forward the key, so the authorisation stays with the caller. Chromium ships exactly this as NonCopyablePassKey. Choose it when the collaborator itself is the authorisation - test seams, migration helpers, one-shot construction - and choose the copyable key when deliberate delegation is part of the design.
pitfalls: Deleting copy and move also means a key cannot be stored or returned; the call must happen where the key was minted.
Passing a non-copyable key by value relies on copy elision (guaranteed since C++17 for prvalues); on C++11/14 keep the parameter by value only where the call site passes a temporary.
Mixing copyable and non-copyable keys for the same restricted operation inverts the delegation guarantee silently; pick one and document it.
